Equation 7 is used to calculate the transition end based on a relative density criterion D where dense gas effects cease to be important when D drops below a value c, c in the range from 0.001 to 0.02 (Hanna, 1989). There are different models which use different D c values. In EPIcode, the D of 0.02 is used (as does the dense gas model DEGADIS). As the D c c value is approached (with increasing downwind distance, x), the density of the plume (air + released gas/aerosol) trends towards ambient temperature and depends primarily on the molecular weight of the released substance. For example, the 0.02 criterion is associated with a volume concentration of 62,000 ppm and 23,000 ppm for CO (MW = 44 g/mole) and Cl (MW = 70 g/mole) respectively. The advantage of comparing EPIcode results to experimental field data is that the field data comes from controlled experiments, which provides a more complete data set of both source and downwind measurements. Therefore, validation is based on the comparison of measured values. In the real-world chlorine release cases, data are limited and based on estimated release parameters (release duration, release geometry, etc.). In this case, EPIcode dense gas validation is run against results from a study by Hanna, et al. (2008), which uses six models to estimate the downwind effects from the actual rail car accidents. All six models used the same scenario data input to get the best model intercomparisons possible. In all models and experimental measurements, the maximum plume depth and width (at select downwind distances and/or centerline concentration target values) clearly show a significant decrease in plume depth and increase in lateral extent (plume width), which is expected when dense gas effects are applicable. Model validation is broken-down into two tasks: • Collection and evaluation of data for use in the validation phase (Section 3.1) • Statistical comparison of EPIcode results to the validation data (Section 3.2) 3.1 Collection and Evaluation of Validation Data The first step in the validation process was the collection and evaluation of potential data for use.
